beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan earns $75,000, and the tax man takes $7,670. Sharma's shares grew $100.0M this year. His tax on that? Nothing. And it's all legal.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. How does a man worth billions pay less tax than me?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Six legal moves. Shares, not salary. Borrow, don't sell. The reset. The foundation. Losers against winners. And the last one, which you can copy.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Move one. Shares, not salary.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Rohan's money arrives as a payslip. Before he even sees it, the tax comes out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: On $75,000 a year, his federal income tax is $7,670. He keeps $67,330.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Every single month. I never even get to touch that part.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A teacher, a nurse, a driver. Everyone paid by payslip lives by the same rule: earn it, and it's taxed.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Even my overtime gets taxed before I see a cent of it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Sharma barely takes a salary. His wealth sits in shares of the company he built.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: This year those shares grew by 10%. On paper, he is $100.0M richer.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: I won't earn that much in my whole life.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the tax on that gain this year? Nothing. In America, a gain on shares is taxed when you sell, not while it grows.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So if he never sells, he never pays?

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Not on the growth. Your tax comes out before you see your pay. Mine waits until I choose to sell.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Why would I pay myself a big salary, beta? Salary is one of the most heavily taxed kinds of money there is.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: When Steve Jobs returned to Apple, he famously took a salary of just a single dollar a year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Income tax on a single dollar a year? Nothing at all. That salary is pure symbolism.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So he worked for free? That's actually kind of noble.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Noble, and clever. His fortune was already in shares. A big salary is taxed every month, at up to 37%.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: One honest detail. Shares paid as wages, like stock awards, are usually taxed as income. The shares a founder started with were never wages.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: That's the gap between earning money and owning things that grow.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So Rohan is taxed on every payslip, before a single dollar reaches him.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And Sharma is taxed on his gains only when he sells, and only when he decides.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's the whole game. A salary gets taxed every month. Shares can grow for decades with no tax on the gain, only on any dividends.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But Sharma still needs cash to live on. Selling would wake the tax man. So he does something stranger.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Move two. Borrow, don't sell.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Sharma wants $100,000,000 to spend. The obvious way is to sell some shares.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: If he sells $100,000,000 of shares that are pure gain, the tax man takes $23.8M.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's 23.8%: the top federal rate on long-term gains, plus the investment surtax.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Sell, and hand over that much? Never. I'll take a loan instead.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The bank hands him a loan of $100,000,000, with his shares pledged as the guarantee.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: The bank lends him that much? They won't even raise my card limit.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Banks like this kind of loan. It's backed by shares they can sell if he ever stops paying.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And here's the trick. A loan is not income. So there is no income tax on it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That borrowed cash pays for the houses, the travel and the parties. None of it counts as income, because it never was.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: But a loan isn't free. He pays interest on every dollar of it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: True. At an assumed 5% a year, the interest is $5.0M a year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Put them side by side. Tax if he sells: $23.8M. Interest for a year: $5.0M. The tax bill is 4.8× bigger, though the interest comes back every year.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: So borrowing beats selling, as long as the shares grow faster than the interest.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Meanwhile the shares he kept keep growing. At an assumed 8% a year, in 10 years they could be worth $215.9M.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The loan costs me interest. The shares earn me more. And the tax man just waits.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The trick was never the loan, beta. The trick is never needing to sell.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the richer you are, the cheaper it gets to borrow. Got it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The catch: if the shares crash, the bank can demand more security, or sell them for him at the worst moment.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Year one, he borrows. Year five, he borrows again. Year ten, his pile is bigger than ever, and he has never sold a share.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Two moves down. But who pays back the loan? That's the strangest move of all.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Move three. The reset.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He buys young. He holds through every crash. He borrows in old age. And then he passes it all on.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Sharma bought his first shares for almost nothing. Today they are worth $1,000,000,000.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Almost every dollar of that is gain. If he sold it all at 23.8%, the tax would be $238.0M.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: So I don't sell. I hold, I borrow, and I keep holding for the rest of my life.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here's why that matters. A gain is measured from your starting price, called the basis. Normally that's what you paid.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: When he passes away, his will leaves the shares to his children.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And their starting price resets to what the shares are worth on that day.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So the gain from his whole lifetime? It is never taxed as a gain. It's wiped clean.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: That can't be legal.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: It is. It's called the step-up in basis, and it's been in the tax code for a century.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: His children could sell the next day and owe almost no capital gains tax.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And all those loans? His estate can pay them off by selling some shares, at the new price, with little gain left to tax.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the loans get repaid, and the gain still never gets taxed. Buy, borrow, die.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Buy, borrow, die. Tax advisers really do call it that.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: There is a catch. Above $15,000,000 per person, the estate can owe estate tax, at up to 40%.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: For most families, estate tax never comes up at all. Their estates are far smaller than that.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And the reset isn't only for the rich. It applies to anyone who inherits, even a small house or a few shares.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Which is why people like me plan for it early. With trusts, and with gifts to charity.

params.name: A gift that stays
params.line: With the family's name on it

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And the most famous of those gifts has the family's own name on the door.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Move four. The foundation.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Three moves done. The fourth starts with a gift.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Sharma gives $500,000,000 of shares to his own family foundation.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: He just gave all of that away?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Why shares and not cash? Cash has already been taxed. Shares full of gain have not.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: A gift is not a sale. So the $119.0M of tax on their gain is never paid.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: And I can deduct the gift from my income, within the limits. Generous, and useful.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: My accountant calls it doing well by doing good.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Bill Gates and Warren Buffett have both given away billions of dollars in shares to foundations.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But the foundation is his family's. His family can run it, and choose where the money goes.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So he gives it away, and somehow still keeps it?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Not quite. By law, it must hand out about 5% of its assets every year in grants. Here, that's $25.0M.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The grants go out. The rest stays invested and can keep growing. And his children can run it after him.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: The money does reach good causes. Slowly, on the family's terms, and with their name on it.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So the rich even get a tax break for being generous. Of course they do.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Four moves down. The next one, he can use every December.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Move five. Losers against winners.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: This year Sharma sold a winner, a stock with $10,000,000 of gain. Tax due: $2.4M.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: But he also owns a loser. A stock that fell by the same amount.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So he sells the loser too, and on paper the loss cancels the gain.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Gain: $10,000,000. Loss: the same. Taxable gain left this year: nothing. His tax bill this year drops by $2.4M.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: And a loss bigger than his gains doesn't vanish. It can carry forward, to cancel gains in later years.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Selling something at a loss, on purpose? That sounds completely backwards.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: The loss was already there. Selling just makes it count. Then I buy something similar, never the same stock within a month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Buy back the same stock too soon, and the rules disallow the loss. It's called the wash-sale rule.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Every December, I look for what's down. Then I put those losses to work.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And this one isn't only for billionaires. Anyone with a taxable investing account can use losses the same way.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Losses are part of investing. This just makes them sting a little less.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So losing money can cut his tax bill. My brain hurts.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's five moves. But look closely at what every single one of them needs.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Every move needs the same thing: a fortune already sitting in shares. Rohan has a payslip. But the last move works with a payslip too.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Move six. The one you can copy.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Billionaires let their money grow untaxed for decades. Ordinary people get a version of that too.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In America it's called a Roth account. You put in money from your pay that's already been taxed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Then it grows. And when you take it out in retirement, if you follow the rules, the growth is tax-free.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The trade is simple. You pay tax on the money going in, so you never pay it on the growth coming out.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Hold on. Someone like me can actually do that?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: So I pay the tax now, while my income is small, and never on decades of growth?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Most people with earned income can, under limits. Other countries have their own versions, like the ISA in Britain.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Many employers also offer a retirement plan at work, and some add money of their own to what you put in.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: I opened mine at your age, with very little. Time did most of the work.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: But a small amount every month can't turn into anything big, can it?

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: It can. And the earlier he starts, the more years the growth gets to work.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Say Rohan puts $500 a month into his nest egg, for 30 years.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: He sets it to move on payday, automatically, so the money is saved before he can spend it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: After 10 years, the pot is $92,083. Most of that is still money he put in himself.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It's move one again, at Rohan's size: money that grows untaxed, for a very long time.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Year one, it's small. Year ten, it starts to grow on its own. By year thirty, the growth is doing most of the work.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Over the years he puts in $180,000. At an assumed 8% a year, it grows to $750,148. And the tax on all that growth, when he takes it out? None.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The catch: there are income limits, a yearly cap on what goes in, and the money is meant to stay put until retirement.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That's $570,148 of growth he never pays tax on. The same idea as the billionaires, at Rohan's size.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: Six moves. Five of them need a fortune. The last one only needs time.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So the rich don't pay less by breaking the rules. They know which money gets taxed, and when.

params.follow: Follow for one money idea a day
params.assumption: US federal tax only, single filer, standard deduction; gains at the top rate with the surtax; loan and growth rates assumed; state tax, fees and inflation left out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Simplified maths: United States federal tax only, with assumed rates. Which move surprised you most? Comment below.
